doc.title: Von Freeman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Chicago repertoire, bands and the end of the big-band era
title: Groups breaking up when members want to be stars
summary: Coleman and Freeman compare big bands to modern groups, with stardom and volume undermining the music.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: You know what this is comparable to? It’s like when you have a group, good group of five people or whatever, and then everybody in the group wants to be a star.
So the group breaks up, and instead of having one strong group of five people, you’ve got five weak groups.

That happens with – it happens with everything. It happened with the Jackson Five. It happened – whatever. You have this group that’s really strong, and then all of a sudden – we used to call it the whispers, when people start whispering, you could make a lot more money if you got out from under so-and-so.
Steve, you got it. You’re hitting it right on the head.
“You need to be on your own. You a star. You need to” – then people start listening to that, and before you know it . . .

I sat there and watched that, because I was in a couple of groups where – I won’t name any names here, because it’s kind of derogative. This cat would be so in power. He would have this group. He had his big name. He’s cutting these records with stars up in New York, but then when you go out on the road, he got to use roadies. He would be so popular. To his dressing room, there would be like 40 women in there, pulling on him. Now how long is he going to last? Next thing you know, that poor man was through. He made the circuit three times intact. So I said, see – whereas before, the band was so popular, there was somebody for everybody.
Yeah, that’s what I was talking about. Like a basketball team. You can’t win with just one cat.

Same difference. It’s just too much. So all those factors – it’s weird, and of course we’re laughing about it, but they were right mixed up into this thing. Like I said, it was the times. So now today – well, it almost wiped out rock too. You get four cats, and here’s a thousand women pulling on them.
It’s definitely stagnated any music. Even if it doesn’t wipe the music out, the music doesn’t develop. You take something like rock. There ain’t been no development in a really long time.

It’s very different, of course, because the volume came in. So instead of getting more talented, you buy another amp and pile it on. You go see four cats, and they make more – the sound is bigger than two or three symphony orchestras put together. And you look up there. It’s four people, and you can’t hear anything, because it’s all these amps hooked up.
The music got – the music has gone through a lot of different things, but invariably it’s got to come back home.
